mainTopic: Guarding documents against forgery, and writing a גט or שובר for one side alone
overview: The amud opens by finishing an earlier discussion about a שטר whose amount can be read two ways. The rule is יד בעל השטר על התחתונה: the holder of the document gets the lower amount. Then אביי gives practical advice against forgery. Never leave your signature at the bottom of a blank page, because a debt could be written above it, and a handwritten IOU can collect. A story shows אביי signing at the top of the page when a sneaky tax collector tried to trick him. אביי also warns not to write the numbers three to ten at the end of a line, where a forger could stretch them into bigger numbers. Three stories follow about forgers who were caught. One turned a ב into a ו, one squeezed in an extra ו, and one faked רבא's signature together with the shaky signature of רב אחא בר אדא. Finally a new משנה teaches that a scribe may write a גט for a husband, or a שובר for a wife, when the other side is not present. He may do this only if he recognizes them, and the husband pays the fee.

steps.title: Unclear amount: the document holder gets the lower sum
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes an earlier discussion. It rules out smaller coins and is left with two readings of the amount. Since the holder of the שטר is at a disadvantage, he collects the smaller one.
steps.simpleTranslation: Smaller coins would have been converted and written as dinars. So what can you say the document means? Either six hundred איסתרי and a dinar, or six hundred dinars and one more dinar. The holder of the document has the weaker hand, so he gets the lower amount.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is wrapping up an argument from the previous page about a שטר whose sum could be read two ways. It decides that the holder of the document collects the smaller amount.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first phrase finishes an earlier point: if the sum were in tiny coins, the writer would have converted them into dinars. That leaves only two possible readings. When we can't tell which one is meant, the creditor holding the שטר must prove his claim, so he gets the lower reading.

keyTerms.meaning: A coin worth less than a dinar
A dinar (זוז), a standard silver coin
The holder of the document (the creditor)
Has the lower hand, meaning he is at a disadvantage

steps.whatToRemember: When the amount in a שטר is unclear, יד בעל השטר על התחתונה: the holder collects the smaller amount.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a basic rule for any document whose wording can be read more than one way. The burden falls on the one who wants to collect.

phrases.english: and he would convert them into dinars;
phrases.notes: This finishes a thought from the previous page: had the sum been in smaller coins, the writer would have turned them into dinars.

phrases.english: what can you say?
six hundred istira and a dinar,
or six hundred dinars and one more dinar?
the hand of the document holder is on the lower side.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the discussion carried over from the previous page about an unclear amount in a שטר.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: When two readings of the sum remain possible, the holder of the שטר collects the lower one.

steps.title: Don't sign at the bottom of a blank page
steps.stepSummary: אביי advises that someone showing his signature in court should not sign at the end of the page. Someone could find it and write a debt above it.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: Someone who needs to show his signature in court should not sign at the bottom of the parchment. Someone else might find it and write above it that the signer owes him money.
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins. אביי gives practical advice on protecting yourself from forgery when you show your signature in court.
steps.deeperAnalysis: People sometimes had to give a sample signature in court so it could be compared with the signature on a document. If that sample sits at the bottom of a blank page, a cheat can fill in the space above it. The result would look like a real IOU in the signer's own hand.

keyTerms.meaning: He is owed money by him

phrases.english: Abaye said:
this one who needs
to show his signature in court,
should not show it at the end of the parchment;
lest another person find it
and write that he owes him money,

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: הַאי מַאן דְּבָעֵי לְמַחְוֵי חֲתִימוּת יְדֵיהּ בְּבֵי דִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new practical teaching about preventing forgery, linked to the theme of document wording.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Do not place a sample signature at the bottom of a blank page, because a debt could be forged above it.

steps.title: Why the forged note would work: a handwritten IOU collects
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a משנה showing that a debt note in the debtor's own handwriting can collect from his free property. So the danger אביי warned about is real.
steps.simpleTranslation: And we learned in a משנה: if someone produces a note in the debtor's own handwriting saying he owes him, the creditor collects from the debtor's free property.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי continues his own statement and backs up his warning with a משנה. It shows that a note written in the debtor's own hand really does let the creditor collect.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without this משנה, you might think a note with no witnesses is worthless, so there is nothing to fear. The משנה shows that a handwritten IOU is valid, at least against property the debtor still owns. A forged debt above a real signature could therefore cost the signer real money.

keyTerms.meaning: Free property, which the debtor still owns and has not sold

phrases.english: and we learned:
phrases.notes: This is a משנה found later in this מסכת, on 175b.

phrases.english: if he presented against him his own handwriting
stating that he owes him,
he collects from free property.
phrases.notes: Free property means what the debtor still owns, not what he already sold to others.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports אביי's warning by showing a handwritten IOU has legal force.
steps.raayaObject: That forging a debt above someone's signature could actually make him pay.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה stating that a note in the debtor's handwriting collects from free property.

steps.title: אביי and the sneaky tax collector
steps.stepSummary: A tax collector asks אביי for a sample signature. אביי signs at the top of the page, the collector tries to pull the page so the signature ends up at the bottom, and אביי tells him the Sages already saw this trick coming.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain tax collector came before אביי and said: Let the master show me his signature, so that when rabbis come and show me a note signed by you, I can let them pass without paying tax. אביי signed at the top of the parchment. The collector kept pulling the page. אביי said to him: The Sages already got ahead of you.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story showing אביי putting his own advice into practice. He signs at the top of the page so no one can write a debt above his name.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The collector's request sounded friendly: he wanted to recognize אביי's signature so he could exempt Torah scholars from tax. When he kept pulling the page, he showed he was really trying to get the signature near the bottom. אביי's answer means the Sages had already warned against exactly this kind of trick.

keyTerms.meaning: They got ahead of you, anticipated you

phrases.english: a certain tax collector
who came before Abaye
said to him:
let the master show me his signature,
so that when rabbis come and show me a note,
phrases.notes: He means a note signed by אביי confirming that they are Torah scholars.

phrases.english: I will let them pass without tax.
He showed it to him at the top of the parchment.
He kept pulling at it,
He said to him: The Sages already got ahead of you.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A story showing אביי's warning about where to sign put into practice.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sign at the top of a page, never at the bottom, so nothing can be added above your signature.
steps.whatToRemember: A signature should never be left at the bottom of a page with empty space above it. Even אביי watched out for this.

steps.title: Don't write the numbers three to ten at the end of a line
steps.stepSummary: אביי teaches that in a document, numbers from three to ten should not be written at the end of a line. A forger could add letters there and make the number bigger.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: Numbers from three until ten should not be written at the end of a line, in case someone forges the document and adds letters.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי gives a second anti-forgery rule, this one about where to place numbers in a document.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Hebrew and Aramaic, adding a short ending to the words for three through ten turns them into thirty through ninety, or twenty in the case of ten. At the end of a line there is empty space where those letters could be slipped in. In the middle of a line, the next word blocks any addition.

keyTerms.meaning: End of a line of writing

phrases.english: Abaye said:
from three until ten,
one should not write them at the end of a line,
lest someone forge and write more.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, separate anti-forgery teaching from אביי.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Numbers three through ten should not be written at the end of a line in a document.

steps.title: What to do if the number lands at the end of a line
steps.stepSummary: If a number from three to ten happens to fall at the end of a line, the writer should repeat the terms two or three times. Eventually the number will fall in the middle of a line.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if it happens that the number falls at the end of a line, he should repeat his words two or three times. It is impossible that the number won't end up in the middle of a line at some point.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי continues his rule and gives a practical fix for when the number lands at the end of a line anyway.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The writer can't always control where a word falls. So instead of erasing, he restates the amount again later in the document. With two or three repetitions, one of them will surely land mid-line, where it can't be forged.

keyTerms.meaning: It happened, it came out that way

steps.whatToRemember: Numbers that can be stretched by adding letters must be protected. Keep them off the end of a line, or repeat them until one lands mid-line.

phrases.english: and if it happens to him that way,
let him repeat his words
two or three times;
it is impossible that it will not happen for him
in the middle of a line.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the fix for when the problem from step 5 can't be avoided.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the number falls at the end of a line, restate the terms two or three times so the number appears mid-line.

steps.title: The forger who turned a ב into a ו
steps.stepSummary: Someone erased the top and bottom lines of a ב so it looked like a ו. That changed 'a third of the orchard' into 'a third, and the orchard.' אביי noticed the extra space around the letter, and the forger admitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: A document said 'one-third of the orchard.' The buyer erased the top and the bottom of the ב, so the word now read 'and the orchard.' The case came to אביי. He asked: 'Why is there so much empty space around this ו?' He pressured the man, and the man admitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a true story of a forgery. It shows the kind of danger אביי warned about in the steps before.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A ב is wider than a ו. So when the forger shaved the ב down into a ו, a gap was left around it. One small letter changed the deal from a third of the orchard to the whole orchard plus a third, but the uneven spacing gave the trick away.

keyTerms.meaning: He tied him up, meaning he pressured him physically

phrases.english: There was a certain document in which it was written:
"One-third of the orchard."
He went and erased the roof of the בית and its foot,
phrases.notes: A ב has a top line and a bottom line. Take both away and only the upright stroke is left, which looks like a ו.

phrases.english: and made it "and the orchard."
It came before אביי.
He said to him: What is the reason
that there is so much room around this ו?
He tied him up, and he admitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a real case of a forger changing letters, after אביי's warnings about forgers adding letters.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Uneven spacing around a letter is a sign that the document was tampered with.

steps.title: The forger who squeezed in an extra ו
steps.stepSummary: A document said 'the portions of ראובן and שמעון, brothers.' The brothers had another brother named אחי. A forger added a ו so it read 'and אחי.' אביי noticed the letters were too crowded, and the forger admitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: A document said 'the portions of ראובן and שמעון, brothers (אחי).' They had a brother whose name was אחי. The man added a ו and made it 'and אחי.' The case came before אביי. He asked: 'Why is this ו so squeezed in?' He pressured the man, and the man admitted.
steps.whatsHappening: A second forgery story. This time the clue is the opposite of the first story: the letters are too close together instead of too far apart.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without vowels, the word for 'brothers' and the name אחי are spelled the same. Adding one ו turned 'brothers' into a third person, so the buyer now owned that brother's share too. Squeezing a letter into a spot where there was no room made the writing look cramped, and that exposed him.

phrases.english: There was a certain document in which it was written:
"The portions of ראובן and שמעון, brothers."
They had a brother whose name was "אחי."
phrases.notes: Written without vowels, 'brothers' and the name אחי look exactly the same.

phrases.english: He went and wrote a ו in it,
and made it "and אחי."
It came before אביי.
He said to him: What is the reason

phrases.aramaic: דְּחִיק לֵיהּ עָלְמָא לְהַאי וָיו כּוּלֵּי הַאי?
phrases.english: that this ו is so crowded?
He tied him up, and he admitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A matching story to step 7, but here the spacing is too tight instead of too wide.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Letters that are crowded together can show that something was added later.

steps.title: רבא recognizes a forged pairing of signatures
steps.stepSummary: A document was signed by רבא and רב אחא בר אדא. רבא said the signature was really his, but he had never signed together with רב אחא בר אדא. The holder of the document admitted it was forged.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a document signed by רבא and רב אחא בר אדא. It came before רבא. He said: 'This is my signature, but I never once signed in front of רב אחא בר אדא!' He pressured the man, and the man admitted.
steps.whatsHappening: A third forgery story. This time the judge is himself one of the 'witnesses' on the document.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The signature looked exactly like רבא's, so the handwriting alone did not give it away. What exposed it was a fact רבא knew: he had never signed any document together with רב אחא בר אדא.

phrases.english: There was a certain document that was signed by
רבא and רב אחא בר אדא.
It came before רבא.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: דֵּין חֲתִימוּת יְדָא דִּידִי הִיא,
phrases.english: He said to him: This is my signature,

phrases.aramaic: מִיהוּ קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב אַחָא בַּר אַדָּא
phrases.english: but in front of רב אחא בר אדא
I never signed!
He tied him up, and he admitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא שְׁטָרָא דַּהֲוָה חֲתִים עֲלֵיהּ רָבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from forged letters inside the text to forged signatures of the witnesses.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A signature can look real and still be forged. Knowing who actually signs together can uncover the fraud.

steps.title: רבא asks how the forger copied a shaky signature
steps.stepSummary: רבא understands how the forger copied his own signature. But רב אחא בר אדא's hands shake, so how could anyone copy his writing?
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: 'I understand that you forged my signature. But רב אחא בר אדא's hands shake. How did you do that?'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא asks the forger a real question about how he did it. This sets up the forger's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An ordinary signature can be copied with practice. A shaky signature has a wobble that is hard to fake on purpose. So רבא wants to know the method.

phrases.english: He said to him: I understand that you forged mine,
but that of רב אחא בר אדא,
whose hand shakes, how did you do it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows up on the forger's confession with a question about his method.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How was a shaky handwriting copied?

steps.title: The forger explains his trick
steps.stepSummary: The forger says he rested his hands on the rope of a swaying bridge while he wrote. Another version says he stood on a wobbly water-skin and wrote.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: 'I rested my hands on a narrow bridge.' Some say: he stood on a water-skin and wrote.
steps.whatsHappening: The forger answers רבא's question. Two versions are given of how he made his own hand shake.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Either way, the trick is the same: write on something unsteady so your hand wobbles naturally, just like רב אחא's. The lesson is that even a hard-to-copy signature can be faked, so judges must stay alert.

keyTerms.meaning: A narrow bridge, often a rope bridge
A water-skin, a leather bag of water

steps.whatToRemember: Forgers can change one letter, squeeze in a letter, or even copy a shaky signature. Judges catch them by watching for odd spacing and by checking facts they know.

phrases.english: He said: I rested my hands on a narrow bridge.
phrases.notes: A swaying bridge, so his hands shook while he wrote.

phrases.english: And some say: he stood on a water-skin and wrote.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He wrote while standing or leaning on something unsteady, so his hand shook naturally.

steps.title: משנה: Writing a גט or a receipt when only one side is present
steps.stepSummary: A scribe may write a גט for a husband even if his wife is not there. He may write a שובר (receipt for her כתובה payment) for a wife even if her husband is not there. The scribe must know who they are, and the husband pays for both.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: A scribe may write a גט for a man even if his wife is not with him. He may write a receipt for a woman even if her husband is not with her. This is only allowed if the scribe recognizes them. The husband pays the scribe's fee.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It teaches when a scribe may write a document for one person while the other side is not there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually we worry that a document written for one side could be misused against the other. Here the scribe may write it for one side alone, but only if he knows the people, so nobody can pretend to be someone else. The משנה also rules that the husband pays for both documents.

keyTerms.meaning: A receipt, here saying the wife was paid her כתובה

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that knowing who the people are protects against fraud. That continues the daf's theme of stopping forgers and imposters.

phrases.english: MISHNA:
One may write a bill of divorce for a man

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין אִשְׁתּוֹ עִמּוֹ,
phrases.english: even though his wife is not with him,
and a receipt for a woman
phrases.notes: This is the receipt she gives when she gets her כתובה money.

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין בַּעְלָהּ עִמָּהּ;
phrases.english: even though her husband is not with her;
provided that he recognizes them.
phrases.notes: 'He' is the scribe, who must know these people.

phrases.english: And the husband pays the fee.

steps.triggerLanguage: כּוֹתְבִין גֵּט לָאִישׁ אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין אִשְׁתּוֹ עִמּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new משנה about writing documents when only one side is present.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A גט may be written for the husband alone and a שובר for the wife alone, as long as the scribe recognizes them. The husband pays for both.
